abstract: Abstract Alternative transcription initiation, which refers to the transcription of a gene from different transcription start sites (TSSs), is prevalent across metazoans and has important biological functions. Although transcriptional regulation has been extensively studied, the mechanism that selects one TSS over others within a gene remains elusive. Using the Cap Analysis of Gene Expression sequencing (CAGE-seq) method, we discovered that Piwi, an RNA-binding protein, regulates TSS usage in at least 87 genes. In piwi -deficient Drosophila ovaries, these genes displayed significantly altered TSS usage (ATU). The regulation of TSS usage occurred in both germline and somatic cells in ovaries, as well as in cultured ovarian somatic cells (OSCs). Correspondingly, RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) initiation and elongation at the TSSs of ATU genes were affected in germline- piwi -knockdown ovaries and piwi -knockdown OSCs. Furthermore, we identified a Facilitates Chromatin Transcription (FACT) complex component, Ssrp, that is essential for mRNA elongation, as a novel interactor of Piwi in the nucleus. Temporally controlled knockdown of ssrp affected TSS usage in ATU genes, whereas overexpression of ssrp partially rescued the TSS usage of ATU genes in piwi mutant ovaries. Thus, Piwi may interact with Ssrp to regulate TSS usage in Drosophila ovaries by affecting Pol II initiation and elongation.

RNA extraction, RNA-seq and RT-qPCR
Ovaries were collected from females in 1× phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and then transferred to TRIzol™ Reagent (Thermo Fisher). RNA was extracted following the manufacturer’s instructions. A total of 10–15 pairs of ovaries were grouped together for each sample. One milligram of total RNA was sent to the Yale Stem Cell Center Genomics Core Facility for RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) library preparation and sequenced at the Yale Center for Genome Analysis (YCGA) with 100 M reads per sample and sequenced using paired-end reads of 150 bp on a NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina). One microgram of total RNA was used for reverse transcription using the High-Capacity complementary DNA (cDNA) Reverse Transcription Kit (Thermo Fisher) following the manufacturer’s instructions, and diluted 20× before quantitative PCR. For quantitative PCR, transcripts of interest were amplified using iTaq

T

Supplementary Table S1
for details about primers and other commercial reagents.
Immunofluorescence
Ovaries from 2–5-day old females were dissected in 1× PBS, then fixed for 20 minutes in fixation solution [0.5% (

Ovaries were then washed three times in PBS with TritonX-100 (PBST, 0.1% TritonX-100 in PBS) for 15 min each and then blocked in 5% normal goat serum (NGS) in PBST for 1 h at room temperature or overnight at 4°C. Blocking solution was replaced with primary antibody diluted in NGS, and samples were incubated overnight at 4°C. Ovaries were washed at room temperature in PBST three times for 15 min each and incubated in secondary antibody diluted in NGS overnight at 4°C. Ovaries were washed in PBST once, then incubated in DAPI diluted in PBST (1:500) for 10 min, and mounted in Vectashield. Samples were imaged using Leica TCS SP5 Spectral Confocal Microscope or Leica Stellaris White Light Lasers. g

g

The tube containing resuspended pellet was vortexed for 30 s, incubated at 37°C for 10 min, and vortexed again to ensure complete solubilization of the pellet. A centrifugation at 14 000
g

After electrophoresis, proteins were visualized by silver staining using the SilverQuest Silver Staining Kit (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. CAGE library preparation and sequencing were performed by DNAFORM. Qualities of total RNA were assessed by Bioanalyzer (Agilent) to ensure that RNA integrity number is over 7.0. The cDNAs were synthesized from total RNA using random primers. The ribose diols in the 5′ cap structures of RNAs were oxidized, and then biotinylated. The biotinylated RNA/cDNAs were selected by streptavidin beads (cap-trapping). After RNA digestion by RNaseONE/H and adaptor ligation to both ends of cDNA, double-stranded cDNA libraries (CAGE libraries) were constructed. CAGE libraries were sequenced using single end reads of 75 nt on a NextSeq 500 instrument (Illumina).
Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing
A total of 50–100 pairs of ovaries were dissected in 1× PBS, then fixed in 1% formaldehyde solution for 10 min at room temperature with rotation. Then, ovaries were quenched with 1/16th volume of 2.5 M glycine for 5 min with rotation, washed in 0.2% TritonX-100 in PBS ×3 for 5 min each, supernatants were removed, and samples were stored at −80°C freezer or proceeded for next steps. The fixed ovaries were gently homogenized in 1× PBS with polypropylene pestle and spun down at 800
g
for 1 min. Supernatants were removed and ovaries were resuspended in 200 μl ChIP lysis buffer [10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM ethylene glycol bis(2-aminoethyl)tetraacetic acid (EGTA), 0.1% Na-deoxycholate, 0.5% N-lauroylsarcosine, 1 mM DTT, 1× protease inhibitor] and transferred to 1.5 ml TPX Plastic Micro Tube (Diagenode) for 10 min sonication using Bioruptor at 30 s ON and 45 s OFF intervals. Chromatin concentration was measured, and chromatin was diluted to achieve <400 ng/μl concentration for additional sonication. Small amounts of sheared chromatin were loaded on 1% agarose gel to check sonication status. Sonication was completed when majority of DNA smears were at 200–500 bp sizes. Sonicated chromatins were incubated with 30 μl of Dynabeads Protein G (Dynabeads) for 1 h at 4°C with rotation to pre-clean the sample. Then, tubes were placed on the magnet and supernatants were transferred to new 1.5 ml tubes. Appropriate antibodies were added into tubes with pre-cleaned chromatin [4 μg of rabbit IgG, or rabbit anti-Pol II Ser5P (ab5131), or rabbit anti-Pol II Ser2P (ab5095)] and incubated overnight at 4°C with rotation. A total of 5% of chromatins were saved as input samples and remaining samples were incubated with 60 μl of Dynabeads for 3 h at 4°C with rotation. Beads were washed four times with 0.2% TritonX-100 in PBS for 5 min each and washed once with TE buffer (10 mM Tris, 0.1 mM EDTA). Tubes were placed on the magnet, supernatants were removed, and chromatin were eluted with 200 μl of elution buffer [50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 10 mM EDTA, 1% SDS] by incubating at 65°C for 15 min. Beads were captured by the magnet and the supernatant from each sample was collected as the immunoprecipitated chromatin. Reverse crosslinking of chromatins was performed by incubating samples at 65°C overnight with 20 μg RNase A (Thermo Fisher) and 40 μg Proteinase K (Thermo Fisher). The DNA was purified using the ChIP DNA Clean & Concentrator kit (Zymo) and then sent to the Yale Stem Cell Center Genomics and Bioinformatics Core for library preparation and sequencing.

Rabbit anti-H3 (ab1791), rabbit anti-Pol II Ser5P (ab5131), rabbit anti-Pol II Ser2P (ab5095) antibodies and rabbit anti-IgG (EpiCypher) were used. The CUT&RUN experiments were performed using the EpiCypher CUTANA ChIC/CUT&RUN Kit (SKU: 14–1048) following manufacture’s protocol with 500K cells per condition. After DNA elution, libraries were prepared using the EpiCypher CUTANA CUT&RUN Library Prep Kit (SKU: 14–1001) and sequenced at the Yale Center for Genome Analysis with about 10M reads per sample.
Bioinformatic analysis of CAGE-seq, piwi-IP small RNA-seq, RNA-seq, chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing and CUT&RUN
CAGE-seq
analysi
s
: CAGE-seq reads were aligned to dm6 genome by STAR 2.7.7 (
40
). Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) reads were removed and only reads that are uniquely aligned with zero or one mismatch were used for downstream analysis. The TSS coordinates were based on the gene annotation file BDGP6.28.101.gff3. For transcripts that share the same starting site, one representative transcript was randomly chosen for the TSS coordinate pool to get rid of the redundancy. To calculate the usage of a TSS of a gene, the reads whose very 5′ end fell within the +15 bp and −100 bp region of the very 5′ end of the TSS were summed and divided by the total reads fell within all non-redundant TSSs for the gene. We only consider the genes who have at least one TSS with ≥10 reads. The usage change was measured by the ratio of the usage in
piwi
mutant against the usage in WT. For the Gene Ontology analysis, we implemented DAVID to CAGE-identified ATU genes to get the enriched terms with
P
-value ≤ 0.05, which were presented as a bar plot by R (
41
,
42
). The expression level change of TSS was calculated by
t
-test. The expression level of a TSS was represented by the total reads whose very 5′ ends fell within the +15 bp and −100 bp region of the very 5′ end of the TSS, normalized by total aligned reads in the corresponding sample. The change of the mRNAs and protein products, caused by altered TSSs, was examined by comparing the isoform/cDNA sequences transcribed from the corresponding TSSs. The ATU genes with the same cDNAs among the isoforms from affected TSSs fell into the category of no peptide change, the ATU genes with different cDNA sequences among the isoforms from affected TSSs were grouped into two categories: peptide change with domain change if there is domain architecture difference among the isoforms from affected TSSs, based on the annotation by SMART, and otherwise peptide change with no domain change (
43
,
44
).
Piwi-IP small RNA-seq:
Piwi-bound piRNAs were collected from five different resources (
30
,
38
,
45–47
). Reads from rrRNAs, transfer RNAs (tRNAs), small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), small nuclear RNA (snRNAs) and microRNAs (miRNAs) were removed based on the alignment from STAR 2.7.7 and 22–32 nt long piRNAs were retained for use. Transposon-derived piRNAs were categorized into LTR, LINE, DNA groups based on whether they overlap with transposons in different groups by ≥1 bp based on RepeatMasker annotation (
48
). piRNA targeting sites were examined within different genomic regions surrounding the usage-changed TSSs by STAR 2.7.7, including the region that is 400 bp upstream of TSSs to 400 bp downstream of TSSs, the region that is 800 bp upstream of TSSs to 800 bp downstream of TSSs and the region that is 1000 bp upstream of TSSs to 1000 bp downstream of TSSs. Two mismatches between the piRNA and the targeting site are allowed. The TSSs of the non-ATU genes served as control here. There is no enrichment for piRNA targeting for the TSSs of ATU genes.
Transposon insertion site analysis:
Transposon insertions were examined within different genomic regions surrounding the usage-changed TSSs, including the region that is 400 bp upstream of TSSs to 400 bp downstream of TSSs, the region that is 800 bp upstream of TSSs to 800 bp downstream of TSSs and the region that is 1000 bp upstream of TSSs to 1000 bp downstream of TSSs.
RNA-seq analysis:
RNA-seq reads were aligned to dm6 genome by STAR (v.2.7.9; settings: – outSAMattributes All –outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate) (
40
). HTSeq was used to quantify transcript level and gene expression for each sample with sorted alignment bam files as input and Drosophila_melanogaster.BDGP6.32.104.gtf as the reference annotation file (
49
). The package DEseq2 was used to perform differential expression analysis with different cutoffs (
P
-value or adjusted
P
-value and fold change) to obtain differentially expressed genes that are statistically significant (
50
).
Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and CUT&RUN analysis:
Adapters were removed from the ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN reads using Trimmomatic, and subsequent reads shorter than 20 nt were discarded (
51
). ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN reads were mapped to the
Drosophila
genome (dm6) using Bowtie 2 allowing 1 mismatch in the seed sequence (
52
). Bigwig files of Pol II Ser5P and Pol II Ser2P were generated using the bamCompare command of deepTools and normalized to input files and then converted to bedGraph files using the UCSC bigwigtobedgraph tool (
53
,
54
). ChIP or CUT&RUN signals at individual genes were visualized using SparK with normalized bedGraph as input files (
55
). Metaplots of ChIP or CUT&RUN signals were generated using the R package metagene2 to specified genomic regions, which are 400 bp upstream of TSSs to 400 bp downstream of TSSs or 1kb upstream to 1kb downstream of TSSs (
56
).

Introduction
Recent advancements in deep sequencing technology have enabled the effective identification of transcription start sites (TSSs) in the genome. For example, the application of Cap Analysis of Gene Expression sequencing (CAGE-seq) for genome-wide mapping of 5′ capped transcripts has aided the systematic identification of TSSs in model organisms such as
Drosophila
, mice and humans (
1
,
2
). These findings revealed the prevalence of alternative transcription initiation (ATI), i.e. the transcription of a gene from different TSSs, in various eukaryotic systems (
3–6
). In humans, >50% of genes are predicted to have alternative promoters, with an average of three putative alternative promoters in a gene (
7
). The usage of alternative start and termination sites more frequently causes mRNA isoform diversity than alternative splicing in human tissues (
8
). These observations imply the importance of ATI in gene regulation.
ATI has important functions in regulating the temporal and spatial specificity of transcription (
8
,
9
), in generating different mRNA 5′UTR sequences with regulatory implications (
10
,
11
), and in producing different isoforms of protein products. For instance, an RNA binding protein in the mouse, Elavl4, has multiple mRNA isoforms, and the translation of specific
Elavl4
mRNA isoforms in early neurons is regulated by the distinct 5′UTR sequences of specific mRNA isoforms (
12
). This contributes to the precise regulation of gene expression during neurodevelopment. For another example, the human gene
LEF1
, which encodes lymphoid enhancer binding factor 1 that regulates β-catenin transcription, has alternative TSSs (
13
,
14
). The resulting
LEF1
transcripts produce two different protein isoforms with opposite functions: the longer isoform recruits β-catenin to Wnt-target genes whereas the shorter isoform misses the β-catenin binding domain and suppresses Wnt-target genes through its interaction with a repressor (
13
,
14
). TSS choices of genes vary among tissues and across developmental stages, indicating that ATI is widely adopted as a form of gene regulation during development (
15
,
16
). Despite the importance of ATI, the majority of alternative TSSs still has unknown functions. Furthermore, it remains unclear how TSSs of these ATI genes are selected in specific cell types or developmental stages.
The choice of TSS for transcription is known to be influenced by the accessibility of regulatory elements such as promoters and enhancers to transcription factors, the recruitment of RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) to specific TSSs, and the rate of its movement through the gene body (
17
). Furthermore, the recruitment of Pol II to specific TSSs is influenced by the presence and DNA-binding activities of transcription factors (
18
,
19
). A recent study investigating alternative promoter usage of the
hunchback
(
hb
) gene in
Drosophila
embryos revealed that the two alternative promoters of
hb
are both active but at different levels in early embryogenesis, and this was proposed to be regulated by the transcription factor, Bicoid (Bcd) (
20
). The first promoter of
hb
requires more cooperative binding of Bcd to two enhancers, whereas the second promoter only requires binding of Bcd to one enhancer for activation (
20
). Overall, the kinetics of transcription factor interactions with promoters and enhancers are key in TSS selection. Despite this knowledge, there are still unknown players and mechanisms involved in selecting and regulating the usage of TSSs for ATI genes. The study of these regulatory mechanisms is essential to understand cell differentiation and cell fate decision.
PIWI proteins form a subfamily of the highly conserved Argonaute/PIWI protein family. They are well known to play important roles in germline stem cell self-renewal and transposon silencing in diverse species such as
Drosophila
,
Caenorhabditis elegans
and mice (
21
). PIWI proteins interact specifically with PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) that are small noncoding RNAs with a typical length of 24–33 nt (
22–26
). The complex and immensely diverse species of piRNAs show sequence complementarity to all major types of sequences in the genome, including transposons, protein-coding genes, long noncoding RNAs and satellite RNAs (
27
,
28
). piRNAs are essential for most regulatory functions of PIWI proteins (
28
,
29
).
In
Drosophila
, there are three PIWI proteins: Argonaute 3 (AGO3), Aubergine (Aub) and Piwi (herein PIWI designates the subfamily whereas Piwi refers to the
Drosophila piwi
gene product). Among them, only Piwi localizes to the nucleus upon piRNA binding (
30
). Previous studies revealed that Piwi can regulate gene expression by affecting the epigenetic states of genomic loci such as Heterochromatin Protein 1a (HP1a) occupancy and H3K9me3 levels, as well as by regulating the accumulation of RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) in these loci (
31–33
).
In most genomic regions, the target-specific regulation of Piwi is achieved by sequence-complementarity between its cognate piRNA and nascent transcripts of target genes (
31
). After binding of the Piwi-piRNA complex to the target genomic site, HP1a is recruited to the same region to initiate epigenetic programming, which is followed by further recruitment of histone methyltransferases such as SU(VAR)3–9 to methylate H3K9 (
32
,
34
,
35
). Recently, it was shown in ovarian somatic cells (OSCs) that, upon loss of Piwi, a strong increase in RNA levels occurred at piRNA-targeted transposable elements (TEs), concomitant with an increase of Pol II occupancy and a decrease of the H3K9me3 level (
33
). Moreover, the expression of many genes is significantly changed (
33
). Several of those differentially expressed genes contain piRNA-targeted TEs nearby (
33
). For example, a
gypsy
insertion in the first intron of the
expanded
(
ex
) locus causes H3K9me3 spreading into the surrounding 10–12 kb genomic region, which covers the TSS of
ex
in wildtype (WT) OSCs (
33
). As a result,
ex
is hardly expressed (
33
). In
piwi-
knockdown OSCs, H3K9me3-marked upstream of the
gypsy
insertion site are completely lost. Correspondingly, the nascent and steady-state
ex
mRNA levels and Pol II occupancy at the

Here, we report that Piwi regulates the usage of individual TSSs of ATI genes in the
Drosophila
ovary. Using CAGE-seq analysis on
piwi
mutants and the WT control, we found that Piwi regulated the TSS usage of ATI genes in germ cells and OSCs, which was confirmed by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) of germline or somatic knockdown of ovarian samples. To investigate the underlying mechanism of Piwi-dependent TSS usage, we conducted genomic profiling of the two active forms of Pol II that are associated with transcription initiation and elongation and discovered changes in both forms of Pol II at TSSs that displayed dysregulated usage upon loss of Piwi. Furthermore, we discovered that Piwi interacts with Ssrp, a Facilitates Chromatin Transcription (FACT) complex component involved in Pol II promoter-proximal pausing and elongation, in the nucleus and showed that Ssrp is involved in regulating TSS usage. We propose that Piwi regulates TSS usage by interacting with Ssrp and affecting Pol II initiation and elongation near TSSs.

68

68

Discussion
In this paper, we have reported a possible novel role of Piwi in regulating the TSS usage of ATI genes, which has important functional implications in producing specific levels and isoforms of mRNAs and proteins. Moreover, our findings on the roles of Ssrp as a Piwi-interactor in this process link Piwi to a transcriptional regulation mechanism and provide a platform for studying how different TSSs within individual genes are selected.
Piwi and Ssrp regulate the TSS usage of ATI genes
Currently, there are only a few studies on how individual TSSs of ATI genes are selected or maintained. In yeast, position of the +1 nucleosome and size of nucleosome-depleted region influence immediately upstream of it regulate the recruitment of the transcriptional machinery and initiation of transcription (
79
,
80
). Yet, the position of +1 nucleosome is often determined by two opposing groups of chromatin remodeler enzymes (
81
). In
Arabidopsis
, as part of the immune response against infection, alternative TSSs are activated (
82
). Despite these exciting discoveries, little is known about what factors are involved in regulating TSS selections and ensuring fidelity of the TSS usage of ATI genes. Our findings on the involvement of Piwi and Ssrp in TSS usage regulation of ATI genes in
Drosophila
bring in new players and a possible mechanism in this regulation, which could be applicable to other systems, as both proteins are highly conserved across organisms.
Piwi regulates TSS usage via affecting the occupancy of initiation- and elongation-associated forms of Pol II near TSSs
It was shown that Piwi can affect the level and distribution of transcription-associated histone marks, such as H3K9me3 and H3K4me2, and subsequently affect Pol II occupancy (
33
,
83
). Our results further revealed that loss of Piwi affected the occupancy of both transcription initiation and elongation associated forms of Pol II near TSSs of ATU genes. This new role of Piwi in TSS usage regulation of protein-coding genes is very different from the well-known function of Piwi in transposon silencing but might be mechanistically related to it and to the epigenetic and transcriptional activation roles of Piwi.
The epigenetic and transcriptional activation roles of PIWI proteins have been reported in different context. In the human breast cancer cell line MCF7, it has been demonstrated that a piRNA derived from a tumor-suppressive long non-coding RNA can upregulate the transcription of TRAIL (
84
). This transcriptional activation is achieved by site-specific recruitment of the hCOMPASS-like complexes by PIWIL1 and PIWIL4 proteins and their interactor WDR5, which result in increased H3K4me3 and decreased H3K27me3 levels near TSS of TRAIL (
84
). In human diffuse large B-cell lymphoma cells, inhibition of a specific piRNA leads to reduced WTAP expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (
85
). This result indicates that this specific piRNA may play an activation role. Most relevant to this study, our lab previously showed that
Drosophila
Piwi is required for the euchromatic state of the telomere-associated sequence at the right arm of chromosome 3 (
47
). These studies are consistent with our finding that Piwi may both activate and suppress transcription.
A number of studies have shown that small RNAs and AGO proteins interact with promoters and TSSs in transcriptional regulation (
86–88
). For example, the AGO1-miR744 complex binds to the promoter of the
Ccnb1
gene that produces Cyclin B1, which increases Pol II and H3K4me3 at the
Ccnb1
TSS in NIH/3T3 cells (
89
). Similarly, the AGO1-miR-320 complex directs the Polycomb group (PcG) component EZH2 and H3K27me3 to the promoter of the cell cycle gene
POLR3D
, which has a
cis-
regulatory role in transcriptional silencing of
POLR3D
(
90
). In addition, AGO1 can also mediate siRNA-directed transcriptional silencing at the promoters of genes coding for human immunodeficiency virus-1 coreceptor CCR5 and tumor suppressor RASSF1A (
91
). Similar mechanisms have also been reported for AGO2 and other miRNAs, siRNAs, and piRNAs (
88
,
92
,
93
). Interestingly, in cultured human cells, AGO1 and AGO2 can even bind to synthetic antigene RNAs complementary to TSS to inhibit transcription (
94
). Piwi, as a member of the Argonaute/PIWI protein family, may act via a similar mechanism to select different TSSs within a gene for preferential use in transcription. Our findings provide basis for further studies to gain new insights in regulatory roles played by the Argonaute/PIWI protein family and small non-coding RNAs in regulating transcription.
Alternative explanations of TSS usage regulation
In addition to its epigenetic role, Piwi is known to repress gene expression through post-transcriptional silencing in cytoplasm as part of the piRNA biogenesis process (
46
,
95
). Recent studies further showed that PIWI-piRNA complexes regulated RNA m
6
A methylation and correspondingly affected RNA stability. For instance, the PIWIL4-piRNA complex was found to interact with an RNA methyltransferase, METTL3, in cardiomyocytes and this interaction blocked METLL3 m
6
A methylation activity (
96
). Increased expression of a specific piRNA (cardiac-hypertrophy-associated piRNA) resulted in decreased m
6
A modification in the
Parp10
mRNA and correspondingly increased PARP10 mRNA and protein levels (
96
). Therefore, Piwi might also regulate specific RNA isoform levels through post-transcriptional regulation. If such regulation indeed exists, it will likely occur during the early post-transcriptional events in the nucleus. Finally, it remains possible that Piwi regulates TSS usage indirectly.
Ssrp regulates TSS usage via affecting the distribution of transcription-associated histone marks
Ssrp is a core component of the FACT complex involved in productive transcription, as shown in diverse systems such as yeast, fly and human (
72
,
73
,
97
,
98
). Recent findings revealed that the FACT complex plays a role in the maintenance of promoter-proximal Pol II pausing in
Drosophila
(
72
). Reduced level of the FACT complex led to redistribution of transcription-associated histone marks H3lysine 4 (H3K4) and H3K36 methylation. These observations support that the FACT complex could be involved in regulating TSS usage of ATU genes through affecting Pol II occupancy near TSSs. Furthermore, Piwi might affect Ssrp distribution on chromatin along with other epigenetic factors to regulate TSS usage.
A working model
It has been reported that Piwi-containing complexes interact with nascent transcripts to anchor themselves to specific genes during transcription (
70
,
99–101
). Combined with the Piwi-Ssrp interaction, we propose that Piwi (possibly with piRNA) binds Ssrp and nascent RNA that is tethered to chromatin (Figure
7
). This facilitates the proper transcription from TSSs of ATU genes in the tethered region that has been selected based on their chromatin context and the presence of transcription factors. In the absence of Piwi, the tethering of the FACT complex to the Piwi-piRNA-bound loci is affected, which would result in changes of Pol II occupancy near TSSs and corresponding changes in TSS usage of ATU genes. At present, the role of piRNA in the regulation is not clear and the role of Ssrp in working cooperatively with Piwi in TSS usage regulation is speculative. In addition, there will likely be other players involved in the Piwi-dependent TSS usage regulation. All these questions await further investigation in the future.
